title: A pyramid tomb where two worlds said goodbye
dek: In Egypt's Western Desert, a small Roman-era pyramid tomb pairs hieroglyphic spells with a 19-line Greek poem for a man named Bisichthes.
body: Out in Egypt's Western Desert, at a site called Bir al-Shughala in the Dakhla Oasis, archaeologists have opened a tomb shaped like a small pyramid. On its stone door, a human figure stands surrounded by protective symbols. Inside, two ways of facing death sit side by side.
The mission belongs to Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, which has been digging at the site since 2002, close to the ancient town of Mothis, beneath modern Mut.

The Egyptian half of the story is carved in stone. The entrance carries a panel of deeply cut hieroglyphs and protective spells, a winged sun disc, bundles of reeds, and a scene from the Amduat, the old royal guide to the sun god's journey through the underworld at night. Nearly three thousand years after the pyramids of Giza, those images were still what a family chose to guard its dead.

The other half is written in Greek: a funerary poem of 19 lines, raised for a man named Bisichthes. The team tentatively believes he served as a judge. The inscription dates to the late third or early fourth century AD, and a bronze coin found in the tomb shows the emperor Constantine, which points to the early fourth century.

Around the burial lay the kit of remembrance: a stone funerary stele with a geometric top, pottery vessels, a sandstone offering table and a basin for purification. Put together, they sketch a household that spoke Greek, lived under Rome, and still wanted the old Egyptian gods to carry its dead safely through the dark.

That is the quiet thread this site keeps following. Knowledge and belief do not vanish when empires change. They are carried, translated and mixed, sometimes for thousands of years, until a desert tomb shows us both at once.
doesnt_show: The announcement gives no full reading of the Greek poem yet, and the idea that Bisichthes was a judge is the team's tentative reading. A scientific publication has not been cited.
settle: A published excavation report with the full Greek text and translation, the tomb's plan and the context of the coin.
